definition:
The kingdom of God is God's rule breaking into a world in rebellion against him to set it right. In one sense God has always been king: “His kingdom rules over all” (Psalm 103:19). But the Bible's story is about that rule being refused by his creatures and then reclaimed, first in Israel and its king, then decisively in Jesus, and finally over the whole creation. Jesus began his public ministry by announcing that “the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15). He taught that the kingdom was present in his own person and work, in his healings, his casting out of demons, and his welcome of sinners, and yet he taught his disciples to pray, “Your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10), because its fullness still lies ahead. Scholars often describe this tension as ‘already and not yet’: the kingdom has come in Christ, is present now wherever his rule is received, and will be complete only when he returns and God is “all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28). The church confesses in the Nicene Creed that Christ's kingdom will have no end.

The Hebrew noun malkut and its relatives mamlakah and melukah mean kingship, reign, or realm; the verb malak means ‘to reign’ or ‘to become king’, and melek is ‘king’. The exact phrase ‘kingdom of God’ is rare in the Old Testament, but the idea is everywhere: God is king, and the cry “The LORD reigns” runs through the Psalms (Psalm 93:1; 97:1). In Daniel the Aramaic malku names the everlasting kingdom God will set up (Daniel 2:44). In the New Testament the Greek basileia can mean a realm, but most often it means kingship or reign, the active exercise of royal power; the German scholar Gustaf Dalman argued this in The Words of Jesus (1898), and most later scholars have agreed. So ‘the kingdom has come near’ means that God has begun to act as king, not that a territory has appeared. Matthew usually says ‘kingdom of heaven’ where the other Gospels say ‘kingdom of God’. Most interpreters see this as a reverent Jewish way of speaking of God by referring to heaven, and not a different kingdom; Jonathan Pennington has argued that Matthew also uses ‘heaven’ to contrast God's rule with earthly kingdoms. The rule of Christ after his resurrection and ascension has its own study (Christ's Ascension and Reign), as do his return and the millennium (The Return of Christ).
ot:
The kingdom begins, in a sense, at creation. God makes humanity in his image “to rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air, over the livestock, and over all the earth” (Genesis 1:26). Human beings were made to govern the world under God, as his representatives. The fall is a revolt against that order, and the rest of Genesis traces the spread of human kingdoms built in defiance of God, from Babel to Egypt, alongside God's promise to Abraham that “kings will descend from you” (Genesis 17:6). The first explicit statement that God reigns comes after the exodus, when Israel sings at the sea, “The LORD will reign forever and ever” (Exodus 15:18). At Sinai God calls Israel to be “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6), a people under his direct rule and representing him to the nations. Balaam hears “the shout of the King” among them (Numbers 23:21), and Moses' blessing says that “the LORD became King in Jeshurun” when the tribes gathered (Deuteronomy 33:5).

Israel's own monarchy was born in tension with this. Gideon refuses the crown: “I will not rule over you, nor will my son. The LORD shall rule over you” (Judges 8:23). When the elders ask Samuel for a king “like all the nations”, God says, “it is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected Me as their king” (1 Samuel 8:7), yet he gives them a king and then chooses David. The covenant with David is the Old Testament's great promise of the kingdom: God will raise up David's offspring and “establish the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Samuel 7:13). Chronicles makes the connection explicit, calling Solomon's throne “the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel” (1 Chronicles 28:5). Israel's king ruled on God's behalf. Psalm 2 imagines the nations raging against “the LORD and against His Anointed One”, while God declares, “I have installed My King on Zion” and promises him “the nations” as his inheritance (Psalm 2:2, 6, 8). Psalm 72 prays that the king will rule with justice for the poor and that his dominion will reach “from sea to sea” (Psalm 72:8).

The Psalms also celebrate God's kingship directly. A group of psalms, 47, 93, and 95 to 99, proclaim “The LORD reigns” and call the whole earth to rejoice, because God “will judge the peoples with equity” (Psalm 96:10). Sigmund Mowinckel argued in the 1920s that these psalms were sung at an annual festival celebrating God's enthronement; others see them as confessing God's eternal reign and anticipating its future display. Psalm 145 praises “the glorious splendor of Your kingdom” and says, “Your kingdom is an everlasting kingdom” (Psalm 145:12-13). The reign of David's house failed. The northern kingdom fell to Assyria in 722 BC, Judah to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC, and the last kings of Judah went into exile. That failure drove the prophets to look for God's own coming reign. Isaiah, who saw “the King, the LORD of Hosts” in the temple (Isaiah 6:5), promises a child who will reign “on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and sustain it with justice and righteousness” with no end to his peace (Isaiah 9:7). He foresees the LORD reigning on Mount Zion (Isaiah 24:23) and a messenger bringing good news to Zion, crying, “Your God reigns!” (Isaiah 52:7). The Greek translation of Isaiah uses the verb for proclaiming good news here, and the New Testament's word ‘gospel’ grows from this language. Jeremiah promises a righteous Branch for David who “will reign wisely as King” (Jeremiah 23:5), and Ezekiel promises that God himself will shepherd his flock through “My servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23-24).

Daniel gives the kingdom its widest horizon. In Nebuchadnezzar's dream a stone cut without hands shatters a statue representing the successive empires, and “the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed” (Daniel 2:44). The proud king himself, humbled, confesses that God's “kingdom endures from generation to generation” (Daniel 4:34). In Daniel 7 four beasts rise from the sea, and then “One like the Son of Man” comes with the clouds and is given “dominion, glory, and kingship”, an “everlasting dominion” (Daniel 7:13-14), which is shared with “the saints of the Most High” (Daniel 7:27). The minor prophets end on the same note. Obadiah closes, “the kingdom will belong to the LORD” (Obadiah 1:21); Zephaniah tells Zion that “Israel's King, the LORD, is among you” (Zephaniah 3:15); Zechariah sees a king coming to Jerusalem “humble and riding on a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9), and a day when “the LORD will become King over all the earth” (Zechariah 14:9). Between the testaments the hope stayed alive. The Psalms of Solomon, from the first century BC, pray for a son of David to drive out the Gentiles and rule Israel in righteousness, and the Mishnah (m. Berakhot 2:2) later describes reciting the Shema as taking on ‘the yoke of the kingdom of heaven’.
nt:
John the Baptist prepared the way: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matthew 3:2). Jesus took up the same announcement and made it the center of his preaching. Mark summarizes his message as “The time is fulfilled” and “the kingdom of God is near” (Mark 1:15), and Matthew calls it “the gospel of the kingdom” (Matthew 4:23). The kingdom is present in what Jesus does. When he casts out demons, he says, “if I drive out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12:28; compare Luke 11:20). Asked when the kingdom would come, he answers that it will not come with signs to be observed, “For you see, the kingdom of God is in your midst” (Luke 17:21). The Greek phrase entos hymōn can mean ‘within you’ or ‘among you’; since Jesus is speaking to Pharisees who oppose him, most modern interpreters take it as ‘among you’, present in Jesus himself, while older readers often took it as an inward reign in the heart. His parables describe the kingdom's hidden and surprising character. It is like seed that grows while the farmer sleeps (Mark 4:26-29), like a tiny mustard seed that becomes a tree and like leaven hidden in flour (Matthew 13:31-33), like a field where wheat and weeds grow together until the harvest (Matthew 13:24-30), and like a treasure worth selling everything to buy (Matthew 13:44).

The kingdom turns the world's order upside down. It belongs to the poor, the mourning, the meek, and the persecuted (Matthew 5:3-10). It must be received “like a little child” (Mark 10:15), and “the tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom of God before you” (Matthew 21:31). Greatness in it means service, “just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:28). Entry requires new birth: “no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again” (John 3:3). And the kingdom is still to come in fullness. Jesus teaches his disciples to pray for it, speaks of the day when many will come from east and west to the banquet with Abraham (Matthew 8:11), tells a parable precisely because some thought the kingdom “would appear imminently” (Luke 19:11), and at the Last Supper says he will not drink wine again “until that day when I drink it anew with you in My Father's kingdom” (Matthew 26:29). At the judgment the King will say, “inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34). A few sayings, such as that some standing there would not taste death before seeing “the kingdom of God arrive with power” (Mark 9:1), have been read as pointing to the transfiguration that follows immediately, to the resurrection and Pentecost, to the fall of Jerusalem, or, by some critics, as a failed prediction of the end.

The kingdom comes by way of the cross. Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9, and is crucified under a sign naming him King of the Jews. Before Pilate he says, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36), meaning that it does not come from the world's sources of power or advance by its weapons, not that it has nothing to do with the world. The dying thief asks, “Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom” (Luke 23:42). After the resurrection Jesus claims “All authority in heaven and on earth” (Matthew 28:18) and spends forty days speaking “about the kingdom of God” (Acts 1:3). When the disciples ask whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel, he answers that the times are the Father's and sends them as witnesses “to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:6-8). Acts shows the apostles preaching “the gospel of the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ” (Acts 8:12), warning that “We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:22), and ends with Paul in Rome proclaiming the kingdom “boldly and freely” (Acts 28:31).

Paul uses the word less often than the Gospels, but the reality is everywhere in his letters, chiefly in the confession that Jesus is Lord. God “has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son” (Colossians 1:13). The kingdom is present as “righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17) and is “not a matter of talk but of power” (1 Corinthians 4:20). It is also an inheritance still to be received, which the unrighteous will not inherit (1 Corinthians 6:9-10) and which “flesh and blood cannot inherit” without resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:50). Christ now reigns, seated “far above all rule and authority” (Ephesians 1:21), and “He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet”; at the end he will hand the kingdom to the Father, “so that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:24-28). Hebrews says believers are “receiving an unshakable kingdom” (Hebrews 12:28), and James says God has chosen the poor “to inherit the kingdom He promised” (James 2:5). Revelation says Christ has made his people “a kingdom, priests to His God and Father” (Revelation 1:6), taking up Exodus 19:6, and that they “will reign upon the earth” (Revelation 5:10). At the seventh trumpet heaven announces, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever” (Revelation 11:15). The story ends with the throne of God and of the Lamb in the midst of a renewed creation, where his servants “will reign forever and ever” (Revelation 22:5). The dominion given to humanity in Genesis 1 is restored in Christ and shared with his people.

keyTexts.why: The first explicit confession that the LORD reigns comes in Israel's song after the exodus. God's kingship is revealed in rescue.
Israel is called to be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation under God's direct rule, a phrase Revelation applies to the church.
Israel's demand for a king like the nations is a rejection of God as king, yet God will work through the monarchy he permits.
God promises David an heir whose kingdom and throne will be established forever, the root of the messianic hope.
The nations rage against the LORD and his Anointed, but God installs his King on Zion and gives him the nations.
God's kingdom is everlasting and its splendor is to be made known to all people.
A child born of David's line will reign with justice and righteousness, and his government and peace will have no end.
The messenger brings good news to Zion that its God reigns, language behind the New Testament's gospel of the kingdom.
The God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shatters the world's empires and stands forever.
One like a son of man receives an everlasting dominion from the Ancient of Days. Jesus' favorite self-description comes from this scene.
Jesus' opening announcement: the time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God is near, calling for repentance and faith.
Jesus' exorcisms show that the kingdom has already come upon his hearers. God's reign is present in Jesus' work.
Parables of the weeds, the mustard seed, and the leaven describe a kingdom that begins hidden and small and grows until the harvest.
Christ reigns now until all enemies, death last of all, are defeated, and then he hands the kingdom to the Father.
The kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, who will reign forever.

history:
The earliest Christian writers expected Christ's kingdom to come visibly on earth. Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho, about 160, chapters 80 and 81) and Irenaeus (Against Heresies, book 5, about 180) looked for a thousand-year reign of Christ with the saints in a rebuilt Jerusalem before the final state. Origen of Alexandria in the third century read the kingdom more inwardly and spiritually and, in his Commentary on Matthew (14.7), called Christ the kingdom itself in person. The creed adopted at Constantinople in 381 added that Christ's kingdom will have no end, rejecting the teaching of Marcellus of Ancyra, who had read 1 Corinthians 15:28 to mean that the Son's reign would one day cease. After Constantine's conversion, Eusebius of Caesarea, in an oration for the emperor's thirtieth anniversary (336), presented the Christian empire as an earthly image of God's heavenly monarchy. Augustine's City of God (413 to 426), written after the sack of Rome in 410, pulled the other way. He distinguished the city of God from every earthly city, including a Christian Rome, and in book 20 he interpreted the thousand-year reign of Revelation 20 as the present reign of Christ in his church, a church that remains mixed, like the field of wheat and weeds, until the harvest.

The medieval West largely followed Augustine, often identifying the kingdom closely with the visible church and its authority. Joachim of Fiore (died 1202) proposed a coming third age of the Spirit, a hope that stirred later radical movements. At the Reformation Luther distinguished God's two ways of ruling, through the gospel in the church and through law and the sword in civil government, in his treatise Temporal Authority (1523). Calvin set out a similar twofold government and treated civil government in the last chapter of the Institutes (book 4, chapter 20). The Anabaptists' Schleitheim Confession (1527) placed the sword outside the perfection of Christ and called believers to separate from it, forming communities that tried to live the Sermon on the Mount. Many Puritans and later Jonathan Edwards held a hopeful postmillennial expectation that the gospel would spread until the kingdom filled the earth. In the Netherlands Abraham Kuyper, opening the Free University of Amsterdam in 1880 with an address on sphere sovereignty, insisted that Christ claims every area of human life.

Modern study of the kingdom began with a controversy. Albrecht Ritschl in the nineteenth century described the kingdom as the moral community of humanity united in love, and Walter Rauschenbusch's A Theology for the Social Gospel (1917) made it the program of Christian social reform. Johannes Weiss, in Jesus' Proclamation of the Kingdom of God (1892), and Albert Schweitzer, in The Quest of the Historical Jesus (1906), argued instead that Jesus expected an imminent, cataclysmic end of the world. C. H. Dodd's The Parables of the Kingdom (1935) answered with ‘realized eschatology’, arguing that for Jesus the kingdom had already arrived. A mediating view then won wide agreement: that the kingdom is both present and future. Geerhardus Vos had argued this in 1903, and it was developed by Werner Georg Kümmel's Promise and Fulfilment (1945 in German), Oscar Cullmann's Christ and Time (1946 in German), Herman Ridderbos's The Coming of the Kingdom (1950 in Dutch), and George Eldon Ladd's Jesus and the Kingdom (1964, revised as The Presence of the Future, 1974). In 1934 the Barmen Declaration of the Confessing Church in Germany rejected the idea that there are areas of life belonging to other lords than Jesus Christ. Jürgen Moltmann's Theology of Hope (1964) made the coming kingdom the horizon of all Christian thought, the Second Vatican Council's Lumen Gentium (1964) described the church as the seed and beginning of the kingdom on earth, and N. T. Wright's Jesus and the Victory of God (1996) read Jesus' kingdom announcement as the promised return of Israel's God to Zion.

differ.view: The church as the seed and beginning of the kingdom
differ.body: Roman Catholic teaching, following Augustine, holds that the church is the kingdom of Christ already present in mystery, what Lumen Gentium (1964) calls the seed and beginning of the kingdom on earth. The kingdom is not simply identical with the church as an institution, but it is truly present and growing in the church through the word, the sacraments, and the life of the saints, and the church's mission is to proclaim and spread it among all peoples. Defenders point to Jesus giving Peter “the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:19) and to Colossians 1:13, and argue that the kingdom must have a visible, historical body if it is truly present in history.

differ.view: The kingdom as God's reign, distinct from the church
differ.body: Many Protestant scholars, including Geerhardus Vos, Herman Ridderbos, and George Eldon Ladd, hold that the kingdom is first God's dynamic reign, while the church is the community of those who have received it. The church witnesses to the kingdom, is created by it, and lives under it, but it is not the kingdom itself, and the kingdom's power is at work beyond the church's walls. Defenders say this distinction keeps the church humble and correctable, prevents any institution from claiming God's authority as its own, and fits the Gospels' use of basileia as reign rather than realm.

Lutheran theology, and a strand of Reformed theology represented today by writers such as David VanDrunen, holds that God rules the world in two ways: through the gospel in Christ's spiritual kingdom, the church, and through law, reason, and the sword in the civil kingdom. Both are God's, but they are not to be confused. The church preaches Christ and administers the sacraments; it does not wield the sword or try to build the kingdom by political means. Defenders point to Jesus' words that his kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36) and that believers should give to Caesar what is Caesar's (Mark 12:17), and they argue that this guards both the gospel from politics and politics from religious tyranny.

Christians in the tradition of Abraham Kuyper, often called neo-Calvinists, hold that because Christ has all authority in heaven and on earth, every area of life (family, work, art, science, economics, politics) is to be brought under his lordship. Believers are not only to save souls but to reform institutions and cultures in keeping with God's creation order, as signs of the coming kingdom. Defenders appeal to the cultural mandate of Genesis 1:28, to texts where Christ is Lord of all (Colossians 1:15-20; Ephesians 1:20-22), and to the renewal of all things (Revelation 21:5). Critics within the tradition warn against confusing any cultural achievement with the kingdom itself, and Kuyper's heirs themselves insist that the kingdom comes fully only with Christ's return.

Dispensational theology, from John Nelson Darby and the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) to its later progressive forms, holds that the Old Testament promises of a Davidic kingdom will be fulfilled literally for the nation of Israel in a future earthly reign of Christ. Classic dispensationalists taught that Jesus offered this kingdom to Israel, that it was postponed when he was rejected, and that the present church age stands between. Progressive dispensationalists, such as Craig Blaising and Darrell Bock, see the Davidic reign as already inaugurated in Christ's resurrection and exaltation, while still expecting a future fulfillment for Israel. Defenders point to Acts 1:6-7, where Jesus does not deny that the kingdom will be restored to Israel but only says the times are the Father's. The debate over the millennium is treated in the study on the Return of Christ.

errors:
The church has rejected any teaching that identifies God's kingdom with a nation, empire, party, or political program. Jesus refused the crown the crowds tried to force on him (John 6:15) and told Pilate his kingdom was not of this world. Whenever Christians have treated an empire, a crusade, or a national cause as the kingdom of God, the result has been to baptize violence and silence the prophets. The church has equally rejected the opposite error, which shrinks the kingdom to a private feeling in the heart with nothing to say about bodies, justice, or the created world. Jesus' kingdom healed the sick, fed the hungry, and forgave sinners, and it ends in a renewed earth, not an escape from it.

Other errors concern timing. One is the conviction that the kingdom will be built by human effort and progress, a hope that many in the social gospel movement held before the First World War and that the war largely shattered; Scripture presents the kingdom as God's gift, received and entered, never manufactured. Another is date-setting and speculation about the end, which Jesus directly forbade (Acts 1:7). A third is the claim that the kingdom is wholly future and has no present reality, which ignores Jesus' own words that it had come upon his hearers. The creeds hold the balance: Christ reigns now, will come again, and his kingdom will have no end.
life:
To pray “Your kingdom come, Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10) is to confess that the world is not yet as it should be and that God has promised to set it right. That prayer shapes a way of life. It means living now under the rule of the King who came to serve, in the upside-down order of the Sermon on the Mount, where the poor are blessed and enemies are loved. It means treating ordinary acts of mercy, forgiveness, honesty, and justice as signs of a kingdom that has already begun.

The doctrine also gives hope and patience. Because the kingdom has come in Jesus, believers need not despair when the world rages; the King has already won. Because it has not yet come in fullness, they need not pretend that everything is fine or try to force the kingdom into being by their own power. They can work, suffer, and wait with the confidence that “He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet” (1 Corinthians 15:25), and that the last enemy, death, will be destroyed.
questions: The Old Testament's first explicit statement that God reigns comes right after the exodus. How does it change your picture of God's kingship that it is first revealed in an act of rescue?
Jesus said the kingdom had come upon his hearers, yet taught them to pray for it to come. Where do you see signs of the kingdom already present, and where do you most long for its coming?
The positions described here differ on how the kingdom relates to the church and to politics. What dangers does each position guard against, and what dangers might each fall into?
